passages.text: Rudbeckia fulgida, the orange coneflower or perennial coneflower, is a species of flowering plant in the family Asteraceae, native to eastern North America.

Description
It is an herbaceous perennial growing up to {{convert|120|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall, with bright yellow daisy-like composite flower heads.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

Growth and reproduction
Rudbeckia fulgida spreads by both stoloniferous stems and seed. The seeds are produced in fruits called cypselae, which are {{convert|2.2|to|4|mm|2}} long and have short coroniform pappi {{convert|0.2|mm|3}} long.
The ripe seed is a favorite food of finches in winter.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

Morphology
{{cn span|Stems are hairy, ridged, and dark green. Leaves are dark green, sparsely but roughly haired, simple, with sparsely serrate margins. [[Flower]]s are heads, with black disk florets and bright orange ray florets, borne singly on stems that extend above the foliage. Stems are glabrous (smooth) or moderately hirsute (hairy) with spreading branches. The leaves have blades that are lanceolate to broadly ovate or elliptic in shape without lobes. The leaf bases are attenuate to cordate in shape and the margins of the leaves are usually entire or serrate, or sometimes lacerate. The upper surfaces of the leaves are glabrous or have hirsute to strigose hairs. The basal leaves are petiolate, with petioles that are {{convert|5|–|30|cm|0}} long and {{convert|1|–|8|cm|1}} wide, the cauline or stem leaves have petioles that are {{convert|2|–|25|cm|1}} long and {{convert|0.5|–|7|cm|1}} wide, the bases are attenuate to cordate or auriculate in shape.|date=September 2024}}

{{cn span|The flower heads are often produced one per stem but are also often produced in corymbiform arrays with 2 to 7 flowers per stem. The cups that hold the flowers called receptacles, are hemispheric to ovoid in shape with [[paleae]] {{convert|2.5|–|4|mm|2}} long, the apices are obtuse to acute in shape with the ends usually glabrous and the apical margins ciliate. The flower heads have 10 to 15 ray florets with laminae elliptic to oblanceolate in shape and {{convert|15|–|25|cm}} long and {{convert|3|–|6|mm}} wide. The abaxially surfaces of the laminae have strigose hairs. The flower discs or center cones are {{convert|12|–|16|mm}} tall and {{convert|10|–|18|mm}} wide, made up of 50 to over 500 disc florets, with the corollas proximally yellowish green and brown-purple distally in color, {{convert|3|–|4.2|mm}} long, having style branches {{convert|1.3|mm|2}} long.|date=September 2024}}

Habitat 
R. fulgida may be found in a variety of habitats such as bogs, woodlands, bottomlands, and calcareous slopes.

Phenology 
This species has been observed to flower from January through September.

Etymology
The Latin specific epithet fulgida means "shining" or "glistening".
The plant is a source of fulgidic acid named after it.

Cultivation
There are seven varieties;
 Rudbeckia fulgida var. deamii (S. F. Blake) Perdue - Deam's coneflower
 Rudbeckia fulgida var. fulgida Aiton - orange coneflower
 Rudbeckia fulgida var. palustris (Eggert ex C.L. Boynt. & Beadle) Perdue - orange coneflower, prairie coneflower
 Rudbeckia fulgida var. spathulata (Michx.) Perdue - orange coneflower
 Rudbeckia fulgida var. speciosa (Wender.) Perdue - orange coneflower
 Rudbeckia fulgida var. sullivantii (C.L. Boynt. & Beadle) Cronquist - Sullivant's coneflower
 Rudbeckia fulgida var. umbrosa (C.L. Boynt. & Beadle) Cronquist - orange coneflower
Rudbeckia fulgida var. deamii and R. fulgida var. sullivantii 'Goldsturm' have both gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.
